content.title: What Is ‘Boy Kibble’? Experts Warn Parents About This Viral TikTok Diet
content.text: Teens may be influenced by social media trends like "boy kibble," which can lead to unhealthy eating habits.A balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats is essential for growing teens.Parents can use these trends as a chance to talk with their teens about nutrition and health in a supportive way. An unpleasant reality of raising modern teens is that they get some of their health advice on social media. Such is the case with a new trend involving what’s being called "boy kibble." Yes, you read that correctly—men are making meals and comparing them to dog food. This dinner in a bowl, however, is less nutritionally complete even compared to what you may be feeding the four-legged members of your family. So, what is boy kibble, and should parents be worried if their teen is trying this trend? What Is Boy Kibble? Some of us are familiar with another social media meal trend called girl dinner, which gained popularity a few years ago. It basically consists of snacks like crackers and cheese, olives, almonds, and other little nibbles that look, well, pretty on a plate. Boy kibble is similarly low on effort, but instead centers around a bowl of rice and ground beef—and not much else. A content creator and International Federation of Bodybuilding Pro named Christian Miles claims he started the trend with one simple Reel. If you look up the trend on TikTok, there are plenty of variations on this basic supper, such as substituting turkey, tuna, or chicken for ground beef. By and large, boy kibble skips variety, without incorporating any veggies or sauce. The goal of scarfing down boy kibble is bulking up post-workout, as well as making meal prep as easy as possible. Indeed, devotees of boy kibble dine on the same combination of rice and meat every single night. Videos show men and teens glorifying boy kibble in such a way that it’s not too difficult to imagine teens following their guidance. But experts are cautioning that getting nutrition recommendations from TikTok has its dangers—as does gobbling up the same grub on repeat. Creators’ Nutritional Notions Should Be Taken With a Grain of Salt Unfortunately, no matter how knowledgeable a TikToker may look and sound online, there may be little science to back up their claims about boy kibble, or any other nutrition topic. "Simply having shoulders that look great in a tank top does not afford someone authority on nutrition," cautions Destini Moody, RD, CSSD, LD, at VNutrition. She says that when it comes to this particular trend, advising followers to eat the same thing is a giant red flag. "Because food is plain, boring, and bland doesn’t mean that it’s healthy and there’s no superior virtue attached to eating this way every night," counsels Moody. "Just because you’re suffering doesn’t mean you’re better, it just means you don’t know better, and that’s not something to look up to in a creator." To be fair, as Madison Szar, MD, pediatrician with Bluebird Kids Health, notes, "Social media can be a great way to connect with experts in a way that was not accessible in the past." But she cautions that the content can also expose teens to information that can be unhealthy, misleading, and even unsafe. Dr. Szar advises making sure claims made on social media include citations and evidence. Why Boy Kibble May Be Dangerous for Teens All diets should include a healthy variety of foods, but this is especially true for growing teens. "One of the first things I noticed about boy kibble is the color, or lack of," says Dr. Szar. She explains that the hallmarks of a nutrient-rich diet include: Fiber Fruits Vegetables Protein Healthy fats Whole grains When your meals lack these essential nutrients, deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids, and micronutrients like calcium, vitamin D, and iron can result. "Additionally, lack of fiber in boy kibble puts kids at risk for constipation and does not support a healthy gut microbiome," says Dr. Szar. Importantly, antioxidants from fruits and vegetables (the color) are missing from boy kibble. "Antioxidants are key to long-term health as they help to reduce inflammation and help vital bodily processes run more smoothly," explains Moody. White rice isn’t the best diet staple either, with Moody noting brown rice, wild rice, or quinoa are higher in fiber and are better choices. "Eating too much white rice can increase the risk of developing type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cause inflammation that could lead to other issues," she says. Finally, ground beef is another questionable choice since it’s high in saturated fat and therefore not heart-healthy. Red meat has been further linked to a higher risk of colorectal cancer when consumed in high amounts, according to Moody. Ultimately, by relying on boy kibble to fill most nutritional needs, teens may end up harming their health and fitness goals, which is the exact opposite of what they are trying to do. Signs Your Teen May Be Obsessed With a Nutrition Trend Like Boy Kibble Enjoying a particular type of meal often is one thing (taco Tuesdays, for instance). But experts agree that if you notice your child eating the exact same thing every single day and night, it’s time to intervene. Other signs to look out for that your teen is not eating a nutritionally sound diet include: Constipation or diarrheaPersistent fatigueNew skin breakouts And while Dr. Szar notes that parents often assume that eating issues pertain only to teen girls, this is not true. "Teenage boys can also be affected by body standards and social media influence that can progress to unhealthy, restrictive eating patterns," she says. If you think your teen is caught up in an unhealthy diet trend, it can be hard to get through to them, especially since their peers or creators they admire may be following the advice. "Some parents feel discouraged when their teens turn to influencers or friends for advice, but this can be an opportunity to open a conversation around health and nutrition," advises Dr. Szar. She encourages parents to approach the discussion from a place of curiosity rather than judgment. Try to gain an understanding of what your child’s concerns are around nutrition and fitness. From there, you can come up with a plan to achieve their goals in a healthy way, involving a nutritionist or pediatrician if necessary. Related Stories
